title: Vinyl Plank in Everett Condos: Sound Ratings, HOA Rules and Underlayment
meta: Vinyl plank in an Everett condo must meet your HOA's IIC sound rating with the right underlayment. Wills Flooring explains the rules, pads and labor cost.
keywords: vinyl plank condo sound rating, LVP underlayment IIC rating, HOA flooring rules vinyl plank, vinyl plank flooring Everett condo, acoustic underlayment for vinyl plank, condo flooring installation Everett WA

blocks.lead: Vinyl plank is one of the easiest floors to get approved in an Everett condo, as long as the plank and underlayment together meet your HOA's sound number, usually IIC 50 or higher, and the board signs off before installation.
blocks.detail: The plank itself is not what passes the test. The underlayment, or the pad bonded to the back of the plank, does the acoustic work. Pick the assembly to match the number in your HOA document and the rest is paperwork and scheduling.

blocks.html: Everett has more condo stock than people expect: the Port Gardner and waterfront buildings, mid-rise units along Colby and Rucker, and the converted apartment complexes around Silver Lake and Eastmont. Most still have builder carpet, and owners want vinyl plank instead. Then the HOA sends over a flooring policy full of acronyms. This post translates it, explains which underlayment does what, and lays out how the job actually runs in a building.

The honest number to compare pads. A Delta IIC of 18 to 22 is typical for quality vinyl plank underlayments.

Ask for a test report on a concrete assembly similar to your building; a bare 6 in slab tests very differently from 8 in with a drywall ceiling.
blocks.note: Ground-floor units and units over parking garages are often exempt. Read your specific policy; two buildings a block apart on Everett's waterfront can require different numbers.

items.title: Attached pad (IXPE or cork backing)
items.text: Many rigid-core planks come with a 1 to 1.5 mm pad already bonded on. Alone it typically reaches the low 50s IIC on a bare slab with a ceiling below. Convenient, but you cannot add a second foam pad under it without voiding most warranties and softening the click joints.

items.title: Separate acoustic underlayment
items.text: A 2 to 3 mm rubber, cork-rubber or dense foam roll under a plank with no attached pad. This is how we hit IIC 55 to 60 requirements. Choose a product rated for rigid vinyl; soft foam meant for laminate lets the joints flex and fail.

items.title: Vapor barrier for older slabs
items.text: Everett's older mid-rise buildings have slabs that were never sealed. A 6 mil poly sheet or an underlayment with a built-in film face protects the plank adhesive and any cork layer. Not a sound product on its own, but often required alongside one.

items.title: Sound-rated adhesive for glue-down
items.text: For glue-down planks, some acoustic adhesives carry their own IIC test data and count toward the rating. Useful in units where the floor height at the entry door cannot rise more than a few millimeters.

blocks.text: Floating or glue-down in a condo?

a.title: Choose this when
items: The HOA rating is met by an attached pad or a rigid-rated roll underlayment
You may sell in a few years and want a floor a future owner can lift
The slab is reasonably flat and dry
Rooms are under about 40 ft in any direction without a transition

b.title: Choose that when
items: Floor height at the entry or balcony door is tight
You want the quietest walk and the least hollow sound
The unit has heavy furniture or a rolling office chair area
The building requires a sound-rated adhesive assembly

blocks.title: Do not stack pads:
blocks.text: The most common failed floor we see in Everett condos is a plank with an attached pad installed over a second foam underlayment because someone wanted extra quiet. The joints rock, the locking strips crack and the warranty is gone. Pick one acoustic layer sized to the number and stop.
Mistakes that fail the sound test or the board

items.html: Submitting the plank's rating instead of the assembly's. A plank box that says IIC 72 was tested with a suspended ceiling below. Your board wants the report that matches a concrete slab.
Using laminate underlayment under rigid vinyl. It is too soft. Rigid core needs a dense, thin pad or the joints flex every time you walk.
Ignoring the perimeter. Plank touching the wall or a nailed baseboard transmits impact noise straight into the structure. The expansion gap is also a sound gap.
Booking the installer before the board answers. Two to four weeks is normal. Order material once you have written approval, not before.

Forgetting the bathrooms and laundry. Most Everett boards treat every room the same, so the sheet vinyl in the bathroom is your chance to unify the whole unit. See our vinyl plank page for the products we bring.

faq.q: What IIC rating does vinyl plank need in a condo?
faq.a: It depends on your HOA policy. Most Everett associations require an assembly rating of IIC 50, and quieter or newer buildings ask for 55 to 60. The plank plus its underlayment must meet that number on a slab like yours, and the test report is what you submit for approval.

faq.q: Does vinyl plank with an attached pad need extra underlayment?
faq.a: Usually not, and stacking a second foam pad under an attached-pad plank voids most warranties and makes the click joints flex. If the attached pad alone does not meet your HOA's number, switch to a plank without a pad and use a rated acoustic underlayment.

faq.q: Can the HOA refuse vinyl plank in my unit?
faq.a: They can refuse a floor that does not meet the sound requirement or was installed without approval. They generally cannot refuse a compliant assembly submitted properly. Ground-floor units are sometimes exempt. Follow the process in writing and keep the approval letter with your closing documents.

faq.q: Is vinyl plank quieter than laminate in a condo?
faq.a: Yes, in most assemblies. Vinyl is denser and less resonant than laminate, so the same underlayment scores a few IIC points higher and the floor sounds less hollow. Glue-down vinyl over a sound-rated adhesive is the quietest option short of carpet.

faq.q: How long does a condo vinyl plank installation take?
faq.a: One to two days for a typical 800 to 1,000 sq ft Everett unit once the board has approved, including tear-out. The approval itself takes two to four weeks, so the calendar is driven by paperwork more than by the installation.
